keyVerseText: Then said Daniel to Melzar, whom the prince of the eunuchs had set over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, Melzar: or, the steward
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מֶלְצָר (meltsâr) is of Persian derivation, likely borrowed from an Assyrian term meaning 'keeper' or 'guardian.' While its exact root is uncertain, the word conveys the sense of a court official entrusted with oversight or stewardship. This etymology enriches the common English gloss 'butler' or 'steward' by emphasizing the role’s responsibility as a guardian or officer in a royal or noble household rather than merely a servant.
usageInScripture: The term מֶלְצָר appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the book of Daniel, where it is consistently used with the definite article, indicating a specific officer. It is translated primarily as 'Melzar' (a proper name) and once as 'the steward,' reflecting the ambiguity of the term's exact function but underscoring a role of authority and care over Daniel and his companions. This limited yet consistent usage highlights the word as a title for a Babylonian court official responsible for overseeing the young men in captivity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מֶלְצָר as a guardian or steward in the Babylonian court invites reflection on God's providential care even within foreign and hostile systems. This word points to the reality that God can work through earthly authorities and their appointed officers to accomplish His purposes. For the Christian faith, it reminds believers that stewardship and guardianship are sacred trusts, reflecting God’s own lordship and care. Moreover, the presence of such a figure in Daniel’s story underscores the theme of faithful witness and divine sovereignty amid exile and trial.
keyVerseReflection: Daniel 1:11 states, 'Then said Daniel to Melzar, whom the prince of the eunuchs had set over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.' Here, מֶלְצָר is rendered as Melzar or steward, identifying the officer charged with their care. This word highlights the human agent through whom Daniel must navigate his captivity, emphasizing the steward’s role as both a guardian and gatekeeper. Recognizing this term enriches our understanding of the context in which Daniel and his friends maintained their faithfulness.
